For more than 15 years, PRTD has used
noninvasive techniques, chief among
them multispectral imaging, on collection
items to glean information invisible to the
human eye. Multispectral imaging involves
digitally photographing an object at multiple
wavelengths.

Through imaging and subsequent processing
of the data it generates, specialists can
obtain information about inks or colorants
used in an object, for example, or detect
a watermark that helps to date it. In some
cases, an ink may almost melt away,
revealing another ink below.

plain_text:
The information uncovered from maps
adds to understanding of how they were
created and of the cartographic practices
of a period. With the Velho portolan, PRTD
brought forward not only place names that
had been illegible, but a scale, numbers
and flags of European claimants to regions.
Scholars mine such details. Place names,
for example, can be used for dating and
can verify that people inhabited a certain
location at a certain time.
